newsitem.title: HUNGARY: VW tops Fiat in central Europe, Daewoo rising fast.
newsitem.headline: VW tops Fiat in central Europe, Daewoo rising fast.

text.p: Volkswagen AG raced past Fiat SPA in March to lead central Europe's booming new auto market, while Daewoo Group just trailed the Italian conglomerate for second place, according to a monthly Reuters survey.
"VW is well-placed to top the region in sales this year, given its strong brand portfolio," David Leggett, an analyst at automotive consultancy CSM Europe, told Reuters.
"Daewoo is very ambitious, and it could finish ahead of Fiat, which has diverted some of its attention from central Europe to focus on strong demand in its home market of Italy."
VW outsold Fiat 20,231 units to 17,966 units in the countries in the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) -- the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
Daewoo, which has become CEFTA's third power by buying several state-owned automakers in the region, vaulted into the fray by boosting sales 49.5 percent in March from February to 17,210 units.
No other automaker sold over 7,000 units in March 1997.
Trailing the Big Three of central Europe were General Motors Corp selling 6,658 units, Renault SA selling 5,317 units, Ford Motor Co selling 4,846 units and PSA Peugeot Citroen selling 4,841 units.
VW -- including the Audi, SEAT, Skoda and VW brands -- overtook Fiat at the end of 1996 and kept a narrow lead in January, before slipping behind the Italian automaker again in February.
Fiat -- including Alfa Romeo, Fiat, Iveco, Lancia and several specialty brands -- had been the annual leader in CEFTA sales from the time the trade pact formed in 1993 until 1995.
The data, based on information that Reuters obtained from a variety of sources, include cars, minibuses, pickups, vans and other four-wheeled motor vehicles not over five tonnes in gross weight.
Overall, CEFTA sales growth remained below its all-time peak in 1996, when sales rose 39.5 percent to 842,577 units.

But the market has started to revive, expanding 25.4 percent to 86,884 units in March 1997 from 69,311 units in March 1996. Year-on-year sales rose only 19.6 percent in February 1997 and 19.7 percent in January 1997.

CEFTA continued to look dynamic compared to western Europe, where year-on-year sales fell 3.0 percent in March 1997, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, known by its French acronym ACEA.
VW has built its lead on a broad presence in the region.
The German automotive group still centers its CEFTA strategy upon Czech brand Skoda, but it also plans to assemble models from each of its brands throughout central Europe.
VW assembles SEATs and Skodas in Poland as well as VWs in Poland and Slovakia. By mid-1998, it plans to start assembling Audis in Hungary.
Fiat has focused more narrowly on CEFTA. It owns the region's biggest car factory in Poland, but it builds no vehicles elsewhere in central Europe.

The Italian conglomerate markets twice as many brands as VW in CEFTA. But many of these brands, such as Ferrari and Maserati, feature high-priced specialty cars that attract only a limited number of customers.
As a result, Fiats accounted for 98.4 percent of the Italian group's sales in central Europe in March, while Skodas represented only 64.3 percent of VW's sales.
Daewoo, which plans to build over 500,000 vehicles a year in central Europe by 2000, has led a Korean blitz on the region in recent years that already has yielded stunning results.
In March, Korean automakers sold 18,400 units in five countries in central Europe, only slightly under the 22,700 units they sold in 18 countries in western Europe.

"The rapidity of Daewoo's actions in central Europe has been startling," Jonathan Storey, director of European Automotive Research Ltd, told Reuters. "Daewoo will force other automakers to re-examine their priorities in this region."
